title: Sync Generators & Iterators
description: function*, yield, Symbol.iterator, Iterable<T>, Iterator<T> — lazy sequences and custom iterables.

challenges.title: What does a generator function return?
challenges.whyMatters: Generators are how you produce values lazily — useful for pagination, chunked file reading, and rate-limited API polling where you don't want to load everything upfront.
hints: function* returns a Generator object — calling next() runs the function until the next yield

choices.label: gen is number[] — all values are computed immediately
gen is Generator<number> — each .next() call resumes execution and returns { value: number, done: boolean }
gen is Promise<number> — generators are always async
gen is an infinite loop that crashes immediately

challenges.title: yield and Generator types
challenges.whyMatters: Understanding the full Generator type lets you build bidirectional generators — useful for coroutines and state machines in complex automation scripts.
hints: T = yielded type, TReturn = final return type, TNext = type sent in via .next(value)

choices.label: T = what yield produces  ·  TReturn = return value when done  ·  TNext = value sent into next()
T = input type  ·  TReturn = output type  ·  TNext = error type
All three are the same type
Generator only has one type parameter

challenges.title: Iterable vs Iterator
challenges.whyMatters: Knowing the distinction prevents confusion when typing custom data structures — an array is Iterable, but the thing you get from array[Symbol.iterator]() is the Iterator.
hints: Iterable has [Symbol.iterator]() which returns an Iterator. Iterator has .next()

choices.label: They are the same — both have .next()
Iterable has [Symbol.iterator]() method — for...of requires Iterable. Iterator has .next() — it is what [Symbol.iterator]() returns
Iterator is for arrays, Iterable is for objects

challenges.title: Write generators for lazy sequences
challenges.description:
Write these generator functions:

1. `range(start: number, end: number, step?: number): Generator<number>` — yields start, start+step, ... up to (not including) end. Default step is 1.

2. `take<T>(iterable: Iterable<T>, n: number): Generator<T>` — yields first n values from any iterable

3. `fibonacci(): Generator<number>` — infinite sequence: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...

All must work with `for...of`.
challenges.whyMatters: range and take are the building blocks of lazy data pipelines — processing the first N results of a paginated API, sampling log entries, generating test data.
hints: range: for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i
take: use for...of on the iterable, yield each, count down
fibonacci: let [a, b] = [0, 1]; while(true) { yield a; [a, b] = [b, a+b] }

challenges.title: Custom iterable with Symbol.iterator
challenges.whyMatters: Custom iterables let you make domain objects — log buffers, service registries, config stores — directly iterable without exposing internal arrays.
hints: Symbol.iterator is the well-known symbol that for...of calls to get an iterator

choices.label: Implement [Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<number> — returning an object with .next()

challenges.title: Write a custom iterable class
challenges.whyMatters: Implementing Iterable on a custom data structure is a real TypeScript skill — and understanding linked list traversal through a generator is a clean example of how generators and iterators compose.
hints: push: walk to the last node (next === null), set its next to the new node
For [Symbol.iterator], use function*: let current = this.head; while (current) { yield current.value; current = current.next }
The return type of [Symbol.iterator] when using a generator is automatically compatible with Iterator<T>

challenges.title: Generator pipeline
challenges.description:
Build a lazy generator pipeline:

- `map<T, U>(iterable: Iterable<T>, fn: (val: T) => U): Generator<U>` — transform each value
- `filter<T>(iterable: Iterable<T>, fn: (val: T) => boolean): Generator<T>` — keep matching values
- `reduce<T, U>(iterable: Iterable<T>, fn: (acc: U, val: T) => U, initial: U): U` — collect to single value
- `pipe<T>(...iterables: Array<Iterable<T>>): Generator<T>` — concatenate multiple iterables

All intermediate functions must be lazy — no intermediate arrays.

Demo: use them together to sum even squares from 1..20.
challenges.whyMatters: Lazy generator pipelines process data without intermediate allocations — essential when dealing with large log files, streaming API results, or memory-constrained environments.
hints: map/filter: function* — use for...of on the iterable inside
reduce: not a generator — just iterate and accumulate
pipe: function* — for (const it of iterables) { yield* it }
Demo: reduce(filter(map(range(1,21), x => x*x), x => x%2===0), (a,b)=>a+b, 0)
